news_posts.post_content:
Ever feel like you’re stuck between junior and mid‑level?

I’ve been there for a year and a half, writing ETL pipelines in Prefect and juggling SQL, Python, BigQuery and Snowflake.

I’ve read DDIA, Fundamentals of Data Engineering, and The Data Warehouse Toolkit, but the pages blur after a few weeks.

What helped me was to stop trying to swallow whole books and start building tiny, focused projects.

First, I revisited system‑design fundamentals with a short primer and applied the concepts to a simple data‑flow diagram for a personal project.

Second, I recreated a dimensional model from the warehouse toolkit using dummy data, just to see the tables and relationships in action.

Third, I set a weekly 30‑minute slot to practice coding interview problems that reinforce CS concepts like indexing and partitioning.

These habits turned abstract theory into muscle memory and gave me confidence in interviews.

- Pick one core topic each week and build a mini‑project around it.
- Keep a cheat sheet of key patterns you use and update it regularly.
- Review your work with a peer or on a forum to get feedback.

What practical steps have you taken to bridge the junior‑mid gap in your data career?

news_posts.post_content:
Ever wonder how universities and industry can truly work together on AI?
Cornell just announced a new Radical Collaboration initiative that brings together leaders from AI and data science.

I’m excited because it shows a shift from siloed research to shared problem solving.
When experts from big tech sit at the same table as academic researchers, ideas move faster.

From my experience, these kinds of partnerships help in three ways:

- Real‑world problems get tackled with the latest academic methods.
- Students gain exposure to industry challenges early in their careers.
- Companies get fresh perspectives that can spark new product ideas.

These collaborations also create a pipeline for talent to move between academia and industry.

If you’re thinking about joining a similar effort, start by identifying a concrete problem you want to solve together.
Set clear goals and keep communication open – that’s how you avoid the usual “talk‑shop” trap.

What collaborations have you found most valuable in your work?

concept_posts.post_content:
Ever found yourself wondering why some users see only their own rows in a QuickSight dashboard?

I ran into that same puzzle last month when a finance team needed each manager to view only their department's expenses.

The solution is Row‑Level Security, or RLS, which lets you attach a filter to a dataset based on the user’s identity.

In practice you create a CSV that maps usernames to allowed values, upload it as a permissions dataset, and then reference that dataset in a custom SQL filter.

Here are a few things I learned while setting it up:

- Define the mapping file once and keep it in S3 so you can version it.
- Use the @{{user}} placeholder in the filter expression to make the rule dynamic.
- Test with a few user accounts before rolling out to the whole org.

A common mistake is forgetting to grant the QuickSight service role read access to the permissions file, which causes the filter to return no data.
